summary.text:
A book that is being deliberately kept short, and is now short. £93.241m of fixed rate debt matures inside twelve months and £68.698m in the year after — £161.939m, 35.4% of the fixed book — and paragraph 2.7 states the policy plainly: 'only take short-dated debt (up to 5 years), due to market conditions, and to refinance for longer periods at the appropriate time'.

The Q4 activity shows what that costs in practice. Maturities came off at 4.10% to 5.30%; the replacements priced at 4.30% to 5.00%, including £20m of PWLB for the HRA at 4.73% over a single year. £120m of new borrowing was taken across the year against a strategy requirement of £118m, and total debt rose from £441.696m to £486.364m.

Investments are thin by design — £44.929m at 3.77%, almost entirely money market funds — because Q4 fixed rates 'were not at levels deemed acceptable to lock in'. Birmingham Airport paid about £2.8m of unbudgeted dividends, which went to the Capital Financing reserve. The appendix carries no CFR by design, so no internal-borrowing figure is recorded; the only statement on it is qualitative, that the HRA is under-borrowed and recharges the General Fund for investment income foregone. No officer is named.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the treasury outturn appendix going to Audit and Risk Assurance on 3 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Scope first. We hold 31 PWLB loans for Sandwell at a balance of £372.2m, inside your £486.364m of total external borrowing. Your appendix does not carry a CFR — it says so, excluding capital expenditure and other long-term liabilities — so nothing below asserts an internal borrowing figure. The only under-borrowing statement in the paper is the qualitative one about the HRA, and we have left it there.

Paragraph 2.7 is the reason we wrote: "The current strategy will remain to only take short-dated debt (up to 5 years), due to market conditions, and to refinance for longer periods at the appropriate time." That is a clear, stated position, and the book now reflects it — £93.241m matures inside twelve months and £68.698m in the year after, £161.939m in total, 35.4% of the fixed book, against indicators of 40% and 30%.

What makes it worth a note is that your own Q4 numbers already show what the strategy costs each time it comes round. Maturities came off at 4.10% to 5.30%; the replacements priced at 4.30% to 5.00%, including £20m of PWLB for the HRA at 4.73% over a single year. So the first roll was broadly cost-neutral. The next one is the question, and it is priced daily rather than annually: one-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26, two-year at 5.06% and five-year at 5.34%.

We have no view on the strategy — "refinance for longer at the appropriate time" is a judgement about the curve and it is yours to make. What we would offer is that the appropriate time is a moving target with an observable price, and that £161.939m rolling inside two years means the decision is effectively continuous. We publish both daily fixings, all three rate bases including the HRA rate you used for that £20m, and the market-implied Bank Rate path from SONIA — currently 4.11% at one year and 4.21% at two against Bank Rate of 3.75%.

The depth side matters as much as the price when a third of a book is rolling. July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One observation from our own data that is unusual enough to mention. Most books we price this year are one-directional, because they were written in one era. Yours is not: 16 loans sit about £24.8m below par and 15 sit about £12.2m above, netting to roughly £12.6m of discount on a £372.2m balance. That near-balance is a direct consequence of the short-dated policy — a lot of the book is priced close to where the curve is now. It is a genuinely different position from most of the sector and worth knowing. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and ours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Two smaller notes. Investments of £44.929m at 3.77% are thin by design, and the £2.8m of unbudgeted Birmingham Airport dividends going to the Capital Financing earmarked reserve is a sensible place for a windfall in a year when £120m of new borrowing was taken against a £118m requirement.

On training, four fit Sandwell. Strategic PWLB borrowing goes straight to 2.7. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting for a book rolling at this pace. HRA treasury & self-financing, given £356.315m of the debt is HRA. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
